title: Pride And Prejudice: Chapter XIX
enhanced_title: Mr. Collins' Proposal: A Study in Delusion and Elizabeth's Defiance
author: Jane Austen
description: This chapter presents Mr. Collins' elaborate, self-serving marriage proposal to Elizabeth Bennet, showcasing his pomposity, Lady Catherine's influence, and Elizabeth's principled rejection despite social pressures.

analysis_entries.paragraph: Mr. Collins' proposal exemplifies Austen's mastery of ironic characterization and satirical prose. His methodical enumeration of reasons for marrying—setting an example for his parish, personal happiness, and Lady Catherine's recommendation—reveals not genuine affection but self-interest and social obligation. The absurdity of his 'violence of my affection' declaration, preceded by calculating paragraphs about entailment and financial practicalities, creates comedic tension that exposes the mercenary nature of many Regency marriages. Austen contrasts Collins' clerical pomposity with Elizabeth's quick wit and moral integrity throughout the scene.
analysis_entries.anchor_text_end_of_sentence:
Having resolved to do it without loss of time, as
his leave of absence extended only to the following Saturday, and having
no feelings of diffidence to make it distressing to himself even at the
moment, he set about it in a very orderly manner, with all the
observances which he supposed a regular part of the business.

analysis_entries.paragraph: The power dynamics between mother and daughter drive the scene's opening drama. Mrs. Bennet's eagerness to secure Elizabeth's compliance—her immediate agreement, her assertion that Lizzy 'can have no objection,' and her maternal insistence—reveals a mother's desperate socio-economic anxiety. The entailment that threatens Longbourn transforms maternal affection into strategic maneuvering. Elizabeth's vexed embarrassment and attempted escape are overridden by her mother's injunction, yet her eventual acquiescence reflects pragmatic wisdom: a moment's consideration making her also sensible that it would be wisest to get it over as soon and as quietly as possible.
analysis_entries.anchor_text_end_of_sentence:
Elizabeth would not oppose such an injunction; and a moment’s
consideration making her also sensible that it would be wisest to get it
over as soon and as quietly as possible, she sat down again, and tried
to conceal, by incessant employment, the feelings which were divided
between distress and diversion.

analysis_entries.paragraph: Lady Catherine de Bourgh casts a long shadow over this proposal, illustrating how aristocratic influence penetrates every level of provincial society. Mr. Collins presents her patronage as a marital asset, describing her unsolicited advice with reverential detail—the quadrille game, Mrs. Jenkinson arranging the footstool, the verbatim quotation of her imperious commands. This absurd deference to rank exposes how the gentry-class clergy internalized aristocratic values. Elizabeth's response—that Lady Catherine would find her in every respect ill qualified for the situation—demonstrates her recognition that Collins' criteria and her own values are fundamentally incompatible.
analysis_entries.anchor_text_end_of_sentence:
Nay, were your friend Lady Catherine to know me, I
am persuaded she would find me in every respect ill qualified for the
situation.

analysis_entries.paragraph: The rhetoric of Mr. Collins' proposal deserves careful analysis as a specimen of Austen's comic genius. His declaration unravels through careful logical exposition: first, why clergy should marry; second, his advantageous situation; third, his connection to Longbourn's entailment. The proposal's climax—his promise of silence about her small fortune—intended as generous forbearance, ironically underscores his complete misunderstanding of romantic language. His insistence that it is usual with young ladies to reject the addresses of the man whom they secretly mean to accept reveals the dangerous assumptions about women that preserved patriarchal structures.
analysis_entries.anchor_text_end_of_sentence:
“I am not now to learn,” replied Mr. Collins, with a formal wave of the
hand, “that it is usual with young ladies to reject the addresses of the
man whom they secretly mean to accept, when he first applies for their
favour; and that sometimes the refusal is repeated a second or even a
third time. I am, therefore, by no means discouraged by what you have
just said, and shall hope to lead you to the altar ere long.”

analysis_entries.paragraph: Elizabeth's refusal tactics evolve throughout the exchange, showcasing her rhetorical skill under pressure. Initial directness ('it is impossible for me to do otherwise than decline them') yields to elaborate self-explanation ('I am the last woman in the world who would make you so') and finally philosophical distinction ('as a rational creature speaking the truth from her heart'). Her repeated insistence on plain speaking—'Can I speak plainer?'—highlights the absurdity that her clarity requires such labor. The contrast between Collins' elaborate circumlocutions and Elizabeth's demand for transparent communication embodies Enlightenment values of reason over social pretense.

The theme of entailment pervades this chapter as both plot device and social critique. Mr. Collins frames his choice of Longbourn daughters as benevolent mitigation of their eventual loss, yet his phrasing—'when the melancholy event takes place'—betrays eager anticipation masked as concern. This economic reality, which makes Mrs. Bennet so desperate and Elizabeth's refusal so risky, illuminates how property law shaped women's destinies. Elizabeth's small portion of one thousand pounds in the 4 per cents., which will not be yours till after your mother's decease, becomes both weapon and vulnerability—Collins' weapon in attempted persuasion, and the economic reason women could not afford principled refusal.
analysis_entries.anchor_text_end_of_sentence:
, which will not be yours till after your mother’s
decease, is all that you may ever be entitled to.

analysis_entries.paragraph: The chapter's conclusion establishes Elizabeth's father as her necessary protector against social coercion. Her determination to apply to her father, whose negative might be uttered in such a manner as must be decisive, reveals Austen's exploration of father-daughter bonds as crucial bulwarks against improper matches. The paternal veto represents one of few avenues of female agency available to women in Austen's world. Mr. Bennet's anticipated behaviour is explicitly contrasted with the affectation and coquetry of an elegant female falsely attributed to Elizabeth, suggesting that authentic masculine authority can recognize genuine feminine rationality where deluded suitors see only strategic flirtation.
analysis_entries.anchor_text_end_of_sentence:
”

To such perseverance in wilful self-deception Elizabeth would make no
reply, and immediately and in silence withdrew; determined, that if he
persisted in considering her repeated refusals as flattering
encouragement, to apply to her father, whose negative might be uttered
in such a manner as must be decisive, and whose behaviour at least could
not be mistaken for the affectation and coquetry of an elegant female.

quote_entries.quote: May I hope, madam, for your interest with your fair daughter Elizabeth, when I solicit for the honour of a private audience with her in the course of this morning?
quote_entries.anchor_text:
Bennet, Elizabeth, and one of the younger girls together, soon
after breakfast, he addressed the mother in these words,--

“May I hope, madam, for your interest with your fair daughter Elizabeth,
when I solicit for the honour of a private audience with her in the
course of this morning?

quote_entries.quote: Dear ma'am, do not go. I beg you will not go. Mr. Collins must excuse me. He can have nothing to say to me that anybody need not hear. I am going away myself.

My reasons for marrying are, first, that I think it a right thing for every clergyman in easy circumstances (like myself) to set the example of matrimony in his parish; secondly, that I am convinced it will add very greatly to my happiness; and, thirdly, which perhaps I ought to have mentioned earlier, that it is the particular advice and recommendation of the very noble lady whom I have the honour of calling patroness.
quote_entries.anchor_text:
Collins, with all his solemn composure, being run away
with by his feelings, made Elizabeth so near laughing that she could not
use the short pause he allowed in any attempt to stop him farther, and

quote_entries.quote: Mr. Collins, you must marry. A clergyman like you must marry. Choose properly, choose a gentlewoman for my sake, and for your own; let her be an active, useful sort of person, not brought up high, but able to make a small income go a good way.
Accept my thanks for the compliment you are paying me. I am very sensible of the honour of your proposals, but it is impossible for me to do otherwise than decline them.

summary: Chapter XIX of Pride and Prejudice presents Mr. Collins' infamous marriage proposal to Elizabeth Bennet, a masterclass in Austen's comic irony and social critique. Through Collins' methodical, self-serving declaration—framed by obligations to his parish, himself, and Lady Catherine de Bourgh—Austen exposes the mercenary nature of many Regency marriages and the grotesque entitlement of mediocre men. Elizabeth's principled refusal, met with Collins' willful misinterpretation as feminine 'delicacy,' highlights the incompatibility between genuine feeling and social performance. The chapter interrogates women's economic vulnerability through the entailment system while celebrating Elizabeth's rational agency and moral integrity, ultimately establishing Mr. Bennet as the necessary arbiter of his daughter's refusal.
